prompt: In `ComputedTotal.vue`, how does the template show the value of `total`?
hint: A computed is a ref, and the template treats a top-level ref in one particular way.

choices.text: `{{ total.value }}`
choices.why: That is how the script reads it. In the template a top-level ref is unwrapped, so `.value` is left out.
A computed is not a function you call; `computed()` returned a ref, and the function inside it is Vue's to run.

choices.text: `{{ total }}`
choices.why: Right. `computed()` returned a ref, and the template unwraps a top-level ref.

choices.text: `{{ total.get() }}`
choices.why: `get` is a key you hand to `computed()` when you want a setter too; the ref it returns has no `get()` to call.

prompt: After one click in the `ComputedTotal` demo, `computing total` was printed once and `totalByHand called` three times. Why the difference?
hint: Count how many times each one is read in the template.

choices.text: The template reads `total` once and calls the function three times
choices.why: The template reads `total` three times too: `{{ total }}`, `total / 60` and `total % 60`. The reads are not the difference.

choices.text: Vue printed the computed's line once to keep the console readable
choices.why: Vue does not filter what `console.log` prints. The function itself ran once.

choices.text: A function in the template runs at each call, on every render; the computed ran once and served its stored result to the other reads
choices.why: Right. The computed is worked out once per change and cached; a plain function has no cache.

choices.text: The computed ran before the click and not after it
choices.why: The transcript prints `computing total` on both sides of `-- click button`: the push changed `sessions`, and it ran again.

prompt: In the planner, which of these are derived and belong in a `computed`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask of each one: could it be worked out from what I already have?

choices.text: The week's total
choices.why: Right. It is a fact about the sessions, not something the student edits.

choices.text: The text typed in a search box
choices.why: Nothing produces that text except the student typing it. It is owned, so it is a `ref`.

choices.text: The courses whose title matches the search
choices.why: Right. It follows from the courses and the text typed.

choices.text: The Monday of the week on screen
choices.why: The buttons choose it and nothing works it out. It is the planner's one new `ref`.

choices.text: The sessions inside the week being shown
choices.why: Right. They follow from the sessions and the Monday.

prompt: In the `LazyComputed` transcript, how many times did the function of `hours` run, from the page opening to the end?
hint: Count the `computing hours` lines.

prompt: In `LazyComputed`, the first click changed `minutes` twice and `hours` was not computed. Why?
hint: Look at the `v-if` on the paragraph that shows it.

choices.text: Vue holds the two writes back and computes on the next tick
choices.why: Batching is about the redraw. A computed is not worked out on a tick, only when something reads it.

choices.text: Nobody had read it: the `v-if` hid the one place that does
choices.why: Right. Lazy means worked out when read, and nothing read it until `Show hours`.

choices.text: `+=` on a ref's `.value` is not seen by Vue's tracking
choices.why: It is seen: the paragraph showing `minutes` redrew, and the next `hours` was worked out from 150.

choices.text: A computed waits for its first change before running
choices.why: There was a change and it still did not run. What starts it is a read.

prompt: A component has `const factor = multiplier.value` at the top of its script, and then `const scaled = computed(() => base.value * factor)`. Later `multiplier.value` changes. What does `scaled` do?
hint: What did the function read while it ran?

choices.text: Recomputes with the new multiplier, because `multiplier` is a ref
choices.why: Being a ref is not enough. The computed depends on what its function reads, and it never read `multiplier`.

choices.text: Vue warns that `factor` is not reactive and recomputes anyway
choices.why: Vue has no way to tell that a plain number was once a ref's value, so there is no warning to give.

choices.text: Goes on using the old value: `factor` is a copy read outside the function
choices.why: Right. Its dependencies are what the last run read, `base` alone, so `multiplier` changing marks nothing stale.

choices.text: Is marked stale, as any ref change in the component marks its computed values
choices.why: Staleness is per dependency. A ref the function did not read leaves it alone.

prompt: A computed runs its function ___: not when its inputs change, but the next time somebody reads it.
hint: One word, an adverb.

prompt: In `WritableHours`, after the first button runs `hours.value = 2`, how many minutes does `minutes` hold?
hint: The setter multiplies by 60 and rounds.

prompt: In `WritableHours`, the second button runs `readOnly.value = 3` on a computed with no setter. What happened, in the development server?
hint: Look for the `[warn]` line and the text of the page after it.

choices.text: A warning, and the value stayed as it was
choices.why: Right. `Write operation failed: computed value is readonly`, and the page still says 120 minutes. A production build drops even the warning.

choices.text: The write went through to `minutes`, and the page showed 180 minutes
choices.why: Writing passes through to the source only when a setter says how. This one has a getter alone.

choices.text: An error stopped the component, and the page went blank
choices.why: The page text is still there after the warning. Vue refused the write and carried on.

choices.text: `readOnly` turned into an ordinary ref holding 3, until the next change
choices.why: A computed does not change into a ref. The write was refused and its value is still worked out from `minutes`.

prompt: Tags are stored as an array `tags` and edited in a text field as `"grammar, verbs"`. The getter is `() => tags.value.join(', ')`. Which setter passes the lesson's test for a writable computed?
hint: After a `set`, the `get` should return what was just written.

choices.text: `(text) => { field.value = text }`, with a ref `field` beside it
choices.why: The getter joins `tags`, which this setter never touches, so a `get` after it shows the old tags. And had the getter read `field`, it would be a ref with extra steps.

choices.text: `(text) => { tags.value.push(text) }`
choices.why: It adds the whole string as one more tag, so writing `"grammar, verbs"` reads back with the old tags in front of it.

choices.text: `(text) => { console.log(text) }`, since the getter already reads `tags`
choices.why: A setter that stores nothing leaves the truth unchanged; the field would snap back to the old tags.

choices.text: `(text) => { tags.value = text.split(', ') }`
choices.why: Right. It turns the view back into the truth, and the getter joins it into the same text again.

prompt: `computed({ get, ___ })` takes two functions, and the second one is what makes it writable.
hint: The key of the function that turns the view back into the truth.

prompt: What did `SyncedByWatch` show on its first render, with two sessions of 45 and 30 minutes?
hint: When does a watcher run for the first time?

choices.text: Planned: 75 minutes
choices.why: That would need the watcher to run when it is created. It runs when its source changes, and nothing had changed.

choices.text: Planned: 0 minutes
choices.why: Right. `total` still held its starting value, 0, while the page had two sessions.

choices.text: Planned: undefined minutes
choices.why: `total` starts as `ref(0)`, so its value is a number from the first line.

choices.text: Planned: 115 minutes
choices.why: 115 came at the end, after the second button had added guitar twice over.

prompt: In `SyncedByWatch`, why did the `push` button not wake the watcher?
hint: What does a watcher on a ref compare?

choices.text: Vue's proxy does not track `push`
choices.why: It does: the computed version notices the `push`, because its `reduce` read every item. The watcher was not looking there.

choices.text: The watcher fired, and its log line was lost behind the render
choices.why: No render line follows the push either, and the total stayed wrong by 20 minutes until the second button.

choices.text: Watchers wait for a second change before they fire
choices.why: The second button woke it at once. It woke because it replaced `.value`, not because it came second.

choices.text: It fires when `.value` is replaced, and `push` changed the array already there
choices.why: Right. That is the second defect; `{ deep: true }` treats the symptom, and a computed removes the copy.

prompt: Which of these are jobs for a watcher rather than a computed? Choose all that apply.
hint: A watcher is for reaching outside the component's own state.

choices.text: Saving the sessions to storage when they change
choices.why: Right. Writing to storage is a side effect.

choices.text: Working out the week's total from the sessions
choices.why: A value that follows from other values is a computed; a watcher here is the lesson's mistake.

choices.text: Fetching a course's details when its id changes
choices.why: Right. A request takes time and reaches outside the component.

choices.text: Keeping a `fullName` ref in step with `first` and `last`
choices.why: If the watcher's body only assigns to another ref, it was a computed all along.

choices.text: Moving focus to a field when an error appears
choices.why: Right. Focus is the page, not the component's state.

prompt: Which of these array methods returns a new array and leaves the one it is called on alone?
hint: Its name says it hands you something back.

choices.text: `sort()`
choices.why: `sort` rearranges the array in place and returns that same array, which is what broke `SortInPlace`.

choices.text: `reverse()`
choices.why: `reverse` changes the array in place, like `sort`; its copy is `toReversed()`.

choices.text: `splice()`
choices.why: `splice` removes and inserts in the array itself; its copy is `toSpliced()`.

choices.text: `toSorted()`
choices.why: Right. It returns a sorted copy, in every browser since 2023 and in Node 20 and later.

prompt: In `SortInPlace`, the line meant to show the data as it was written came out sorted. Why?
hint: Which of the two computed values changed something it read?

choices.text: `toSorted()` sorts the original as well, and only the return is a copy
choices.why: `toSorted()` leaves the original alone; that is the whole reason the lesson recommends it.

choices.text: `byDateWrong` called `sort` on `sessions.value` itself
choices.why: Right. `sort` rearranged the original array through the proxy, and every reader of `sessions` saw the new order.

choices.text: The template sorts a list of dates before printing it
choices.why: A template prints what the expression returns. The `first` line confirms the data was written with the 23rd first.

choices.text: The two computed values share a cache, so the first line read the sorted copy
choices.why: Each computed has its own cache, and the first line reads `sessions`, not either computed.

prompt: `AsyncComputed` gives `computed()` an `async` function that fetches `/courses.json` and returns the status. What happened?
hint: What does an `async` function return?

choices.text: The page showed 200 once the request answered
choices.why: A computed does not wait for a promise. Its value is the promise itself.

choices.text: The page printed `"[object Promise]"`, and the request was not sent
choices.why: The function did run, so the `fetch` went out; its answer went nowhere.

choices.text: The page printed `"[object Promise]"`, and the request ran anyway
choices.why: Right. The value is the promise, and the template printed it the one way it prints an object.

choices.text: Vue warned that a computed cannot be `async` and showed nothing
choices.why: The transcript has no warning at all. Nothing told anybody, which is the danger.

prompt: Which of these computed bodies breaks the rule that a computed only reads and returns?
hint: Look for a method that changes the array it is called on.

choices.text: `() => [...items.value].reverse()`
choices.why: `reverse` changes an array in place, but this one is the fresh copy the spread just made.

choices.text: `() => items.value.filter((i) => i.done)`
choices.why: `filter` returns a new array and leaves `items` as it was.

choices.text: `() => items.value.reverse()`
choices.why: Right. It turns `items` itself around, and every other reader sees it reversed.

choices.text: `() => items.value.length`
choices.why: Reading a length changes nothing.

prompt: What is the one new piece of state `App.vue` gains in this section?
hint: Everything else on the screen is worked out from it and from the sessions.

choices.text: `total`
choices.why: `total` is a computed, worked out from the sessions and the Monday.

choices.text: `perCourse`
choices.why: `perCourse` is a computed: each course with its own totals.

choices.text: `monday`
choices.why: Right. `ref(weekStart(new Date()))`, and the two buttons replace it.

choices.text: `weekTotal`
choices.why: `weekTotal` is a plain function in `planner.js` and holds no state.

prompt: `sessionsInWeek` writes `s.date >= monday && s.date <= sunday` with no `Date` object in sight. Why does that compare dates correctly?
hint: What form are the dates kept in?

choices.text: JavaScript turns both strings into dates before comparing
choices.why: `>=` on two strings compares them as text. It works because of the form the text is in.

choices.text: `YYYY-MM-DD` sorts as text in the order of the dates
choices.why: Right. Year, then month, then day, each padded, so text order is date order.

choices.text: `monday` is a ref, and Vue compares a ref's value as a date
choices.why: Inside `planner.js` nothing knows about Vue; `monday` arrives as a plain string.

choices.text: The comparison is approximate, which is close enough for a week of sessions
choices.why: It is exact for every date in that form; the session of the 12th is left out of the week of the 19th, as the header shows.

prompt: With the clock on 21 October 2026, the header said `75 of 195 minutes done`. What is the 195?
hint: `weekTotal` filters before it adds.

choices.text: The minutes of every session in the file, the 12th included
choices.why: The session of the 12th is not in the week of 19 October; with it the total would be 245.

choices.text: The goals of the three courses added together
choices.why: The goals are 180, 120 and 90, which make 390, and the header does not read them.

choices.text: The minutes planned in that week
choices.why: Right. Five sessions from Monday the 19th to Sunday the 25th: 45, 30, 60, 20 and 40.

choices.text: The minutes planned this week and the one before it
choices.why: One week back the header says 50 of 50, so the two weeks together would be 245.

prompt: A search box keeps its results with `watch(query, (q) => { matches.value = courses.value.filter((c) => c.title.includes(q)) })`. The courses arrive from `fetch` a moment after the page opens. What goes wrong?
hint: What is the watcher's source, and what else does the result depend on?

choices.text: Nothing: the watcher runs once when it is created, so `matches` starts filled
choices.why: A watcher runs when its source changes, not when it is created; that was the first render of `SyncedByWatch`.

choices.text: The list stays empty until somebody types, since the watcher is on `query` and not on the courses
choices.why: Right. A computed over `query` and `courses` would be right on the first read and follow both.

choices.text: It needs `{ deep: true }` before it notices the typing
choices.why: Typing replaces the string in `query.value`, which a plain watcher sees. What it misses is the courses.

choices.text: `filter` changes `courses` in place, and the list shrinks with each search
choices.why: `filter` returns a new array; it is `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` that change the original.

prompt: Which of these could be the body of a computed without breaking its rule? Choose all that apply.
hint: Could you call it ten times in a row, or not at all, and have the page be the same?

choices.text: `[...sessions.value].sort(byDate)`
choices.why: Right. The copy is sorted, and `sessions` keeps its order.

choices.text: `localStorage.setItem('total', t)`, then return `t`
choices.why: Writing to storage is a side effect at a moment nobody chose. It belongs in a watcher.

choices.text: `weekTotal(sessions.value, monday.value)`
choices.why: Right. `weekTotal` reads its input and returns a new object.

choices.text: `sessions.value.push(extra)`, then return the length
choices.why: `push` changes the array the computed reads, and every reader of `sessions` gets the extra session.

choices.text: `sessions.value.filter((s) => s.done).length`
choices.why: Right. Filtering makes a new array and counting it changes nothing.
